name: Undulating periodization (DUP)

lead: Undulating periodization changes the training stimulus frequently, in daily undulating periodization (DUP) from workout to workout, for example a heavy low-rep day, a moderate day and a lighter high-rep day for the same lift in one week. It is a way of organising resistance training to keep making strength and size gains.

Its payoff for looks is more muscle and strength over time. Systematic reviews comparing it with linear periodization have found similar results for strength and muscle size, so people choose it for variety and preference.

paras: Lifters rotate rep ranges and intensities across sessions in a weekly template, keeping total weekly work similar. Variations include flexible DUP, where the day's intensity is chosen by how the lifter feels. Programs are usually run for weeks to months before being changed.

Resistance training carries general injury risks from poor technique or excessive load, and training that is too heavy or too frequent can cause overuse problems. No safety issues are specific to undulating schedules.

angle.text: DUP is a way to schedule training, so the appearance benefit comes through more muscle and strength built over months. Lifters use it to train different rep ranges weekly and to avoid repeating the same workout.

lead: Undulating periodization, abbreviated DUP when the variation happens day to day, is a resistance-training approach that alternates training volume and intensity across sessions instead of progressing steadily from high volume to high intensity over months [1]. A typical week for one lift might include a heavy low-repetition session, a moderate session and a lighter higher-repetition session. It is popular among people building muscle and strength because it lets several qualities be trained each week and gives variety, and for appearance purposes the payoff comes through the muscle and strength built over months of consistent training [2][3].

Periodization as a concept draws on Hans Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome; Leo Matveyev formalised the model around 1964, and Tudor Bompa expanded it [1]. Undulating models were studied in the early 2000s, when Rhea and colleagues reported that a daily undulating program produced larger strength gains than a linear program with equated volume and intensity in a 12-week trial of 20 men [4]. Later trials and meta-analyses have mostly found the two approaches produce similar results.

A 2015 meta-analysis of 17 studies with 510 participants found both approaches increased strength with no difference between them in upper- or lower-body strength [2]. A 2017 meta-analysis of 13 trials found a standardised mean difference of -0.02 for muscle hypertrophy between linear and daily undulating models [3]. A 2022 meta-analysis of 35 studies found periodisation of volume-equated training favoured periodised over non-periodised programs for maximal strength, with no difference for hypertrophy, and favoured undulating over linear programs for strength only in trained participants [5].

paras: In linear periodization training moves in phases, usually starting with higher volume and lower load and ending with lower volume and higher load. In undulating models the stimulus changes more often, in DUP at each session [1]. A typical week for one lift might include a heavy session, a moderate session and a lighter higher-repetition session, while total weekly volume is often kept similar.

Reviews of short-term periodization describe undulating strategies as rotating program variables such as volume, intensity and exercise selection in a biweekly, weekly or daily fashion [6]. A review of drug-tested classic powerlifting describes a hypertrophy-power-strength model with daily undulating periodization three times a week on non-consecutive days for squat and bench press [7].

sections.h: Variants and how lifters use it
paras: Variants described in studies include traditional DUP with prescribed loads, flexible DUP, in which the lifter selects the day's intensity according to readiness, and modified DUP with different volume distributions across days [8][9]. Rating of perceived exertion and repetitions-in-reserve scales have been used to set loads in periodized programs [10].

Lifters use it for physique goals by rotating rep ranges across the week for each muscle group or lift, so that a heavy day trains strength, a middle day trains a moderate range and a lighter day trains higher repetitions that are commonly associated with hypertrophy [6].

On T Nation, members describe DUP in their training logs; one wrote that varied rep ranges and weights "made training extra fun" while their lifts and size rose [11]. Another thread summarises a coach's view that debating which periodization model is best matters less than experiencing several [12]. Other posters mention DUP variations within published programmes, such as a DUP template from a Tactical Barbell book and a DUP variation of a programme called Operator [13][14].

Wikipedia describes periodization as drawing on Selye's stress-adaptation model, formalised by Matveyev around 1964 and expanded by Bompa [1]. Garhammer published one of the first US articles on periodizing strength training in 1979, and Soviet periodization information was shared with American strength coaches in the 1980s [1].

Rhea and colleagues' 2002 and 2003 trials compared linear and daily undulating programs with equated volume and intensity: the 2002 trial in 20 men found larger strength gains for DUP [4], and the 2003 trial of 60 adults over 15 weeks found no significant differences in muscular endurance gains among linear, DUP and reverse-linear groups [15].
Critics such as Kiely argue that supporting studies compared varied training with unvaried training and did not show how variation should be scheduled [1].

A 2015 meta-analysis of 17 studies (510 participants) found that sixteen reported significant strength increases for both linear and undulating approaches and found no difference between them; the authors noted that short study duration and participants' training history may confound results and that variety may help further gains [2].

A 2017 meta-analysis of 13 trials found no meaningful difference between linear periodization and DUP for muscle hypertrophy (Cohen's d -0.02; 95 percent confidence interval -0.25 to 0.21) [3]. The 2022 Sports Medicine meta-analysis of 35 studies reported effect sizes of 0.31 favouring periodized over non-periodized training for 1RM strength, 0.13 for hypertrophy (not significant), and no hypertrophy difference between linear and undulating models (0.05) [5]. For undulating versus linear strength, the effect was 0.31 overall and 0.61 in trained participants, with no difference in untrained ones [5].

Umbrella reviews of resistance-training variables summarise the broader picture: one of 14 meta-analyses covering 178 primary studies and 4,784 participants suggested at least 10 sets per muscle group per week for hypertrophy [16], and another of 44 systematic reviews found resistance training consistently increased muscle mass, strength and physical function in healthy adults [17].

Rhea et al. (2002) randomised 20 men for 12 weeks and reported greater strength gains in the DUP group at mid-test and post-test [4]. Miranda et al. (2011) randomised 20 resistance-trained men for 12 weeks; both models improved 1RM and 8RM leg press and bench press without significant difference, though DUP had larger effect sizes [18]. Klemp et al. (2016) compared high- and low-repetition volume-equated DUP programs in 16 trained men over 8 weeks and found similar strength and muscle thickness gains [19].

Zourdos et al. (2016) compared a modified DUP with a traditional configuration in 18 powerlifters over 6 weeks; the modified model gave greater total volume and a larger bench press 1RM gain, with squat and deadlift differences not significant [8]. Colquhoun et al. (2017) randomised 25 trained men for 9 weeks to flexible or traditional DUP; both improved on all lifts, fat-free mass rose about 0.8 kg in each group, and motivation and satisfaction did not differ [9]. Helms et al. (2018) found similar results with RPE-based and percentage-based loading in 21 trained men over 8 weeks [10].

Pelzer et al. (2017) trained one leg of 19 women with traditional periodization and the other with DUP for 6 weeks; knee extensor 1RM rose 18 and 24 percent and muscle thickness 12-20 and 13-19 percent respectively, without significant difference [20]. Painter et al. (2012) compared block with daily undulating training in 31 Division I track and field athletes over 10 weeks, finding no significant strength differences but calculated efficiency favouring block training [21].

Trials have also examined undulating programs in other populations, including older women, older adults and people living with HIV [22][23][24], and a 2026 meta-analysis of 29 studies reported comparable effects of linear and undulating training on athletic capacity, body composition and glucose regulation, with undulating training favoured for lean mass in obese participants [25].

Trials are generally short, often 6 to 15 weeks, and use small samples, and reviewers highlight that participants' training status and the equating of volume affect conclusions [2][5]. Kiely has argued that benefits attributed to periodization schedules may reflect variation itself rather than a specific sequence [1].
Resistance training carries general injury risks from poor technique or excessive load, and heavy or very frequent sessions can contribute to overuse problems.

lore.intro: On T Nation and similar lifting forums, DUP is discussed as one of several ways to organise a training week, often alongside linear, block and conjugate approaches [12][26].

claims.claim: Changing rep ranges every session keeps progress going and prevents stagnation.
DUP builds more muscle than linear programming.
DUP is better for trained lifters' strength.
Flexible or autoregulated DUP lets you train by feel without losing gains.
The best periodization model is settled by debate.

Garhammer publishes one of the first US articles on periodizing strength training.[1]
